name: Attention Weight Analysis
description: Attention weight analysis inspects the weights an attention-based neural network computes for an input, to see which input positions the model draws on as it builds each part of its output. In recurrent encoder-decoder models, such as early neural machine translation, the weights for each output step form an alignment matrix over the source tokens, which is plotted as a heatmap and read as a soft alignment between source and target. In transformers, each attention head (one of several parallel attention units in a layer) produces its own matrix of how strongly every token attends to every other token; the analyst extracts these matrices from the model, for example by asking a Hugging Face model to return its attentions, and views them per head and layer or aggregates them over many inputs to characterise what individual heads do. The output is a set of heatmaps and head-level summaries showing how information is routed inside the model; on its own it does not measure how much each input contributed to the prediction.

example_use_cases.description: A localisation team validating an in-house neural translation model for equipment manuals plots the encoder-decoder attention matrix for a sample of sentences and checks that each translated term attends to its source counterpart, sending sentences whose attention collapses onto punctuation or end-of-sentence tokens for human review.

A team assessing an image-captioning model for an alt-text service overlays each generated word's attention weights on the image to check that words such as 'wheelchair' or 'crossing' fall on the matching objects, and records captions whose nouns attend mainly to background regions.

A clinical NLP team reviewing a transformer that extracts medication details from discharge letters uses head and model views on a sample of letters to find heads that link each drug name to its dose and frequency, then checks whether those heads behave the same way on letters from a second hospital before describing them in the model documentation.

A model-risk team reviewing a contract-clause classifier uses attention maps as a first look at which phrases the model draws on, then tests the highlighted phrases with an attribution or ablation method before reporting them, because its validation policy does not accept attention weights alone as evidence of what drove a decision.

limitations.description: Attention weights are not a measure of feature importance. Across several text tasks, attention weights often disagreed with gradient-based importance, and quite different attention distributions produced the same prediction; a reply showed the verdict depends on the test used. Treat a heatmap as a hypothesis to confirm with attribution or ablation, not as the reason for a decision.

In transformers, residual connections and stacked layers mix information from different tokens, so one layer's weights do not show which input tokens a later representation depends on. Raw attention agreed less well with ablation and gradient importance than aggregates across layers such as attention rollout, which are themselves approximations.

A transformer produces one matrix per head per layer for every input, often well over a hundred, and many heads attend mostly to delimiter tokens such as the separator. Saying what a head does requires aggregating over many inputs, and a few hand-picked examples can suggest patterns that do not hold across the data.

Applies only to models that compute attention explicitly, and the meaning of the weights depends on the mechanism: an encoder-decoder alignment over source words is not the same object as self-attention among tokens of one sequence. Head roles found in one model or domain do not carry over to another, so the analysis must be repeated for each model assessed.

resources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
resources.abstract: Neural machine translation is a recently proposed approach to machine translation. Unlike the traditional statistical machine translation, the neural machine translation aims at building a single neural network that can be jointly tuned to maximize the translation performance. The models proposed recently for neural machine translation often belong to a family of encoder-decoders and consists of an encoder that encodes a source sentence into a fixed-length vector from which a decoder generates a translation. In this paper, we conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of this basic encoder-decoder architecture, and propose to extend this by allowing a model to automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word, without having to form these parts as a hard segment explicitly. With this new approach, we achieve a translation performance comparable to the existing state-of-the-art phrase-based system on the task of English-to-French translation. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that the (soft-)alignments found by the model agree well with our intuition.

What Does BERT Look At? An Analysis of BERT's Attention
resources.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

resources.title: Attention is not Explanation
resources.abstract: Attention mechanisms have seen wide adoption in neural NLP models. In addition to improving predictive performance, these are often touted as affording transparency: models equipped with attention provide a distribution over attended-to input units, and this is often presented (at least implicitly) as communicating the relative importance of inputs. However, it is unclear what relationship exists between attention weights and model outputs. In this work we perform extensive experiments across a variety of NLP tasks that aim to assess the degree to which attention weights provide meaningful “explanations” for predictions. We find that they largely do not. For example, learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based measures of feature importance, and one can identify very different attention distributions that nonetheless yield equivalent predictions. Our findings show that standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations and should not be treated as though they do.

sample_claims.text: For the sampled sentences, the translation model's encoder-decoder attention aligns each translated technical term with its source term, and sentences where it does not were reviewed by a translator
The captioning model's attention for each generated object noun falls on the corresponding object in the image for the reviewed sample of alt-text outputs
The attention heads identified as linking drug names to doses behave consistently across discharge letters from both hospitals in the validation set
Phrases that attention maps suggested were decisive for the clause classifier were confirmed by an independent attribution method before being reported to reviewers
